title: Private Deployments: VPC & On-Prem Deployment Guide, Day-2 Ops, Upgrade and Rollback, and Customer Requirements Library
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Purpose
This consolidated guide explains Redwood Inference private deployment patterns (VPC-hosted and on-prem), reference architectures, packaging requirements, Day-2 operational runbooks, and formal upgrade and rollback procedures. It also contains a customer requirements checklist used by Solutions and Professional Services during pre-sales and onboarding. Target audience: platform engineers, SREs, customer engineers, and solutions architects executing or supporting private deployments.

Scope
- VPC-based private deployments (customer VPC with private connectivity)
- On-prem (air-gapped or restricted networks) packaging and installation constraints
- Reference architectures for small, medium, and large footprints (development, production, high-availability)
- Day-2 ops tasks: monitoring, backups, scaling, capacity planning, security patching
- Upgrade and rollback playbooks with pre-checks, staged rollouts, and post-upgrade validation
- Customer requirements library and checklist for procurement/engagement

High-level architecture overview
- Control plane options: Redwood-managed control plane (with customer allowlist) or customer-managed control plane for stricter environments.
- Data plane: Hosts model inference containers on customer GPU instances (on-prem or cloud). Traffic flows are strictly inbound/outbound per deployment model.
- Key components: API gateway (TLS & mTLS), inference workers (GPU), model registry & storage (S3-compatible), config and secrets store (Vault/KMS), observability stack (Prometheus/Grafana), autoscaler, and load balancer.

Reference architectures (short)
1) Development (single AZ / single host):
   - 1 control plane endpoint, 1 inference node (8-16 vCPU, 64-128 GB, 1x GPU T4/A10G).
   - Use for PoC, very low capacity, no HA.

2) Production, medium footprint (recommended starting profile):
   - HA control plane across 2 AZs, 2 inference nodes per AZ (2x A10G or equivalent), dedicated logging/metrics nodes.
   - Load balancer with session affinity disabled, autoscaler configured for target latency SLO (95th percentile).

3) Production, high-availability, high-throughput:
   - Multi-region control plane (optional), 3+ inference nodes per AZ, cross-AZ KV cache replication, model cache tiering (SSD local cache), and GPU pooling per model profile.

Network & security requirements
- Required: outbound HTTPS to Redwood control plane endpoints (if using Redwood-managed control plane) on 443; if customer-managed control plane, public egress can be locked down.
- mTLS: API gateway and inference nodes support mutual TLS; customer must provide certs or use integrated Vault CA.
- Firewall rules: allow internal control plane <-> data plane ports (by default 8443 for control-plane RPC, 9090 for metrics, 12345 for inter-worker RPC).
- Private DNS: recommended entries for service discovery (api.redwood.local, model-registry.local).
- KMS/HSM integration: network connectivity to customer KMS (AWS KMS endpoint, Azure KeyVault, or on-prem HSM) for envelope encryption.

Hardware and baseline capacity guidance
- Minimum for production: 2x NVIDIA A10G (or equivalent), 64 GB RAM per worker, 1 Gbps NIC, 500 GB NVMe for model cache.
- Preferred for inference latency-sensitive workloads: 4x A100/A800 per cluster with PCIe 4.0 NVMe, 200 GB swap offload disabled.
- Disk: model cache tiered: local NVMe (hot) + NFS/SMB or S3-compatible (warm).

Packaging & on-prem install patterns
- Distribution formats: OCI images for components; Helm charts for Kubernetes-based installs; tarball + systemd recipes for bare-metal (air-gapped).
- Air-gap process: provide signed OCI bundles via offline registry artifact + checksum and GPG signature. Customer runs local registry import script.
- Installation modes:
  - Kubernetes (recommended): Helm chart values explained below.
  - Systemd container mode: systemd unit templates and a bootstrap script.

Helm values (example, specified as text snippet):
- global.domain: "redwood.local"
- controlPlane.replicas: "3"
- worker.gpuEnabled: "true"
- worker.resources.requests.cpu: "4000m"
- worker.resources.requests.memory: "64Gi"
- storage.modelCache.size: "500Gi"
- ingress.tls.mode: "mtls"
- observability.prometheus.enabled: "true"

Day-2 operations checklist (daily/weekly/monthly cadence)
Daily:
- Check SLO dashboard for 95p/99p latency and error rate.
- Verify model registry sync status and sufficient cache hit rate (>60% target depending on workload).
- Validate queue/backlog length (requests in flight) is within configured autoscaler thresholds.
- Headline health: api-gateway, control-plane leader, all workers Up.

Weekly:
- Rotate short-lived certificates (if using internal CA).
- Verify backup snapshots for model artifacts and Postgres/config store.
- Review cost & utilization dashboard: GPU utilization, average tokens/sec, host CPU/mem.

Monthly:
- Run canary workloads for model correctness and latency regression detection.
- Security patching window for OS and container runtime.
- Capacity planning review with forecasted growth and reservation recommendations.

Monitoring & observability (what to watch)
- Metrics: request_latency_ms{p95,p99}, tokens_per_second, gpu_utilization, model_cache_hit_rate, error_rate.
- Alerts (examples):
  - High latency alert: p95_latency > configured_slo for 5m -> Severity P1
  - Model sync failed: model_registry_sync_success == 0 -> P2
  - GPU OOMs: gpu_oom_count > 0 in 10m -> P1
- Dashboards: per-model latency heatmap, per-worker GPU utilization, global QPS & tail latency.

Backups & recovery
- Config DB (Postgres): nightly logical backups + WAL shipping (retention 14 days default).
- Model artifacts: periodic snapshot to S3-compatible object store (incremental).
- Recovery runbook: restore DB to point-in-time, rehydrate model cache from snapshot, validate service health, and bring traffic back via LB.

Upgrade procedure (recommended phased rollout)
Pre-upgrade checks:
1) Ensure backups completed and verified (DB snapshot, model artifacts).
2) Verify health of all nodes and 0 pending critical alerts.
3) Record current config and image digests.
4) Confirm rollback image is available on nodes.

Staged rollout steps (Kubernetes example):
1) Tag release and publish to registry (immutable tag).
2) Canary: update 5% of workers (or 1 node) with new image and run smoke tests (latency, deterministic prompts).
3) Monitor canary for at least 30-60 minutes for error/regression signals.
4) Progressive rollout: 25% -> 50% -> 100% with pauses and automated health checks at each step.
5) If any stage fails automated checks, trigger automated rollback to previous image and notify oncall.

Upgrade rollback procedure
Fast rollback (on failure detected during rollout):
- Immediately scale new image replicas to 0 for the affected subset and redeploy previous image tag.
- Re-route traffic away from canary nodes via LB.
- If state migration was performed, execute state rollback steps documented for that migration (see migration manifest).
Post-rollback validation:
- Re-run smoke tests and confirm SLOs.
- Capture logs and traces for RCA; open incident/ticket and notify stakeholders.

Upgrade notes for stateful components
- Database schema migrations: must be backward compatible or follow a multi-step deploy (write-compatible migration -> deploy new code -> finalize migration).
- Model cache format changes: ensure versioned cache paths so old cache can co-exist until warmed.

Common failure modes and mitigation
- GPU OOM after upgrade: reduce batch size or revert to previous runtime; increase GPU memory limits and re-run canary.
- Registry mismatch in air-gapped: validate checksum/GPG and re-import bundle.
- DNS/service discovery failure: check kube-dns/consul, fallback to static hostfile entries.

Operational runbook (incident starter)
1) Triage: determine scope (single node, cluster, all regions).
2) Temporarily shift critical traffic to fallback model variant or Redwood-hosted fallback if configured.
3) Collect logs and traces: API gateway, control-plane leader, and affected worker(s).
4) If worker-level resources are exhausted, restart worker after capturing OOM traces; if persistent, scale horizontally.
5) Post-incident: complete PCR and update runbook with root cause and remediation.

Customer requirements library (onboarding checklist)
- Network:
  - Allowed egress destinations (control plane endpoints or Redwood-mirror registry).
  - Subnet, routing, and firewall rules for worker-to-worker and control plane ports.
- Identity & secrets:
  - KMS access details (endpoint, principal), Vault/secret engine access, and cert signing policy.
- Storage:
  - S3-compatible endpoint and credentials for model artifacts, required capacity estimate, and performance profile (IOPS).
- Hardware:
  - GPU model and count, host CPU, RAM, NVMe size, and network bandwidth.
- Compliance & data residency:
  - Required region, logging retention limits, and sensitive data isolation needs.
- Operations:
  - Oncall rotation contacts, maintenance windows, and escalation paths.
- Access:
  - Admin users list, RBAC matrix for observability, model registry, and deployment actions.

Templates (examples to provide to customers)
- Network ACL template (CIDR rules), Helm values example, systemd unit example, and offline-registry import steps (copy/pasteable).
- Example smoke test: curl -sS --cert client.crt --key client.key https://api.redwood.local/v1/health | jq

Ownership and escalation
- Primary owner: eng-private-deployments team (oncall rotation).
- Support escalation: customer-success -> solutions-engineering -> eng-private-deployments -> eng-sre.
- SLA expectations: documented during commercial contract; default internal SLO for private deployment operability: 99.5% uptime monthly for control-plane, 99.0% for data-plane inference availability (customer-specific SLA overrides in contracts).

Appendix: Useful CLI snippets
- Check worker status (kubernetes): kubectl get pods -l app=redwood-worker -o wide
- Fetch logs: kubectl logs -l app=redwood-worker --since=1h
- Rehydrate model cache (example): rwdctl cache restore --source s3://customer-models/snap-2026-02-28 --concurrency 4
